extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Proving and working with equivalence relations, equivalence classes, partitions, and functions; includes standard definitions and proof strategies (existence/uniqueness, subset inclusions, lemma use, composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation iff it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check each property separately (verify (x,x) ∈ R for reflexivity; if (x,y) ∈ R then (y,x) ∈ R for symmetry; if (x,y) ∈ R and (y,z) ∈ R then (x,z) ∈ R for transitivity). Examples: same-birthday relation, congruence modulo m (Cm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an equivalence class
rubrics_metrics.description: For x ∈ A, the equivalence class [x] is the set of elements related to x (i.e., [x] = { y ∈ A | y R x }).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequences: x ∈ [x]; if x ∈ [y] then [x] = [y]. Use the definition repeatedly when proving containment or equality of classes; examples illustrate shapes of classes (e.g., fractional parts, congruence classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes partition the set (A/R is a partition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is an equivalence relation on A, then the set A/R of all equivalence classes is a partition of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove A/R is a partition show the three clauses of the partition definition: (1) union of classes equals A (∀x∈A show x∈[x]); (2) classes are pairwise disjoint (if X,Y∈A/R and X≠Y then X∩Y=∅); (3) each class is nonempty (each contains its representative). The text suggests proving pairwise disjointness by proving the contrapositive: assume intersection nonempty then show equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set equality by mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets S and T are equal, prove S ⊆ T and T ⊆ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each inclusion is typically proved by taking an arbitrary element of one set and showing it belongs to the other (the arbitrary-element method). This method is used repeatedly (e.g., to prove [y] = [x] by proving [y]⊆[x] and [x]⊆[y]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving subset inclusion: arbitrary-element method
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove U ⊆ V, let z be an arbitrary element of U and prove z ∈ V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write out definitions (e.g., membership in an equivalence class means a relation pair holds) and use properties (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity) as needed. The text repeatedly models this pattern in lemmas and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the contrapositive for negative conditionals (pairwise disjointness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving implications whose antecedent or consequent is a negative statement (e.g., X≠Y → X∩Y=∅), it can be easier to prove the contrapositive: assume X∩Y ≠ ∅ and prove X = Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'is empty' is negative, proving the contrapositive lets you introduce witnesses from existential givens and apply lemmas (as in the proof that equivalence classes are pairwise disjoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing an equivalence relation from a partition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a partition F of A, define R = ∪_{X∈F} (X × X). This R is an equivalence relation on A (the relation determined by F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity directly from the definition of R and the partition properties. Lemmas are recommended: first show reflexivity (every x lies in some X∈F so (x,x)∈R), then leave the rest for exercises or prove similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation determined by partition yields same classes
rubrics_metrics.description: If R = ∪_{X∈F} (X × X ) and X ∈ F with x ∈ X, then the equivalence class [x]_R equals X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove [x]_R ⊆ X by taking arbitrary y ∈ [x]_R and using existential instantiation to find the Y∈F that witnesses (y,x)∈Y×Y; use disjointness of F to deduce Y=X. Prove X ⊆ [x]_R directly by observing (y,x)∈X×X for y∈X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of congruence modulo m
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive integer m and integers x,y: x ≡ y (mod m) iff ∃k∈Z (x−y = k m); equivalently m | (x−y). The relation C_m = {(x,y)∈Z×Z | x ≡ y (mod m)} is an equivalence relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check properties: reflexivity and symmetry are routine (exercise), transitivity follows by adding divisible differences (exercise reference). Use congruence classes (residue classes) as examples of equivalence classes; count number of classes for Cm (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of function as a special relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation F ⊆ A×B is a function from A to B (written F:A→B) iff ∀a∈A ∃! b∈B ((a,b)∈F) — for every a there is exactly one b with (a,b) in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: each a∈A is paired with a unique element f(a)∈B. Domain must be all of A; range (image) is Ran(f) = { f(a) | a∈A } and may be a proper subset of B. Examples and non-examples illustrate failures (not paired, or paired with multiple outputs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying functions by rules must cover entire domain
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a function by a rule (e.g., f(x)=x^2+7), the rule must determine f(a) for every a∈A (implicit universal quantification is accepted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the author states 'let f:R→R be defined by f(x)=x^2+7' it is understood the formula applies to all x∈R; you may plug any real number into the expression. Failure to define values for all domain elements invalidates the function definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of functions via pointwise equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are functions from A to B and ∀a∈A (f(a)=g(a)), then f = g (as sets of ordered pairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof method: show f ⊆ g and g ⊆ f by taking arbitrary (a,b)∈f, deducing b=f(a)=g(a), so (a,b)∈g, and vice versa. This gives a standard technique for proving two functions are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of functions is a function and evaluation formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:A→B and g:B→C then g∘f : A→C and (g∘f)(a) = g(f(a)) for each a∈A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by showing existence and uniqueness: existence by letting b=f(a) and c=g(b) to get (a,c)∈g∘f; uniqueness by assuming two possible c's arise and using uniqueness in f and g to deduce equality. Use this to compute examples and derive formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence-and-uniqueness proof pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement of the form ∃!x P(x) (there exists a unique x with property P), prove existence and uniqueness separately: construct a witness for existence; for uniqueness assume two witnesses and show they are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern is used in proving composition is a function, proving ∃!b in function definition, etc. The text explicitly separates existence and uniqueness steps and demonstrates typical constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lemmas to structure proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove auxiliary facts (lemmas) primarily to make the proof of a larger theorem easier and clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates proving Lemma 4.6.5 and Lemma 4.6.7 before Theorems 4.6.4 and 4.6.6. Strategy: identify reusable facts, prove them as lemmas, then cite them in the main proof to simplify reasoning and avoid repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential instantiation when working with unions/unions of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition or hypothesis yields an existential statement (e.g., R = ∪_{X∈F} (X×X) gives (x,x) ∈ R means ∃X∈F ((x,x)∈X×X)), introduce a witness variable (choose an appropriate X) to continue the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used repeatedly: after letting x be arbitrary and using ∪F = A, choose X∈F with x∈X; similarly, from (y,x)∈R get Y∈F with (y,x)∈Y×Y. The commentary emphasizes recognizing existential goals and instantiating witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain vs. range of a function
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A→B the domain is A (every a∈A appears as first coordinate of exactly one pair in f); range Ran(f) = { f(a) | a∈A } is a subset of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When specifying a function, check that every domain element is assigned a value; the range need not equal B. Use the notation f(a) and set-builder description f = { (a,b) ∈ A×B | b = f(a) } when convenient.
